blocks.content: Every device on your home network has an IP address, but that address is not the same kind of address the rest of the internet uses to find your router in the first place. Public and private IP addresses are two genuinely different categories, solving two genuinely different problems, and understanding the split is essential for making sense of how your own home network actually works.

This topic builds directly on the ipv4-vs-ipv6 topic address scarcity problem, and sets up the NAT topic later in this module, which is exactly the mechanism that bridges these two categories together.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437539707-633163028.png
1. Two Genuinely Different Kinds of Addresses
blocks.text: 1. Two Genuinely Different Kinds of Addresses

blocks.content: A public IP address is unique across the ENTIRE internet, no two devices anywhere in the world are supposed to share one at the same time. A private IP address is only unique within one single local network, your home, your office, and it has no meaning at all to anything outside that specific network.

2. A Real, Concrete Example: Your Own Home Network
blocks.text: 2. A Real, Concrete Example: Your Own Home Network

blocks.content: Your router has exactly one public IP address, assigned by your internet provider, that represents your entire home to the rest of the internet. Every individual device inside your home, your laptop, your phone, your smart TV, gets its own private IP address instead, assigned by the router itself, and only meaningful within your own home network.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437539707-854445256.png
blocks.alt: A Real, Concrete Example: Your Own Home Network

blocks.content: 3. The Reserved Private IP Ranges

Three specific ranges of IPv4 addresses are permanently set aside, by agreement across the entire internet, specifically for private, local use. Any device anywhere is free to use an address from these ranges on its own local network, since they are never handed out as public addresses at all.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437541161-640456302.png

4. Why the Same Private Address Can Be Reused Everywhere
blocks.text: 4. Why the Same Private Address Can Be Reused Everywhere

blocks.content: Since private addresses only need to be unique within their own local network, the exact same private address, 192.168.1.10 for instance, can be, and genuinely is, in use on millions of completely different home networks around the world at the same time, with zero conflict at all. Your neighbor router almost certainly hands out some of the exact same private addresses yours does.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437541161-254828241.png
blocks.alt: Why the Same Private Address Can Be Reused Everywhere

blocks.title: Why this actually works
blocks.content: A private address only ever needs to be distinguished from other devices on its OWN local network. Since two different local networks never directly see each other traffic at this level, reusing the same private ranges everywhere causes no real world confusion at all.
5. Private Addresses Are Not Reachable From Outside
blocks.text: 5. Private Addresses Are Not Reachable From Outside

blocks.content: A private IP address is genuinely not routable on the public internet at all. If someone outside your home tried to directly send data to 192.168.1.10, it would simply fail, that address means nothing outside the context of your own specific local network.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437541162-55162063.png
blocks.alt: Private Addresses Are Not Reachable From Outside

blocks.title: This is actually a real security benefit too
blocks.content: Devices behind a private network are naturally shielded from being directly reachable by anything outside, since outside traffic has no route straight to a private address at all. This is a genuine, practical side benefit of the private addressing scheme, not just an addressing technicality.
6. NAT: The Bridge Between the Two
blocks.text: 6. NAT: The Bridge Between the Two

blocks.content: So how does a device with only a private address ever actually reach the public internet at all? Network Address Translation, covered in complete depth in its own dedicated topic later in this module, is exactly the mechanism that translates traffic between a device private address and the router single public address, letting every device on your private network share that one public identity when talking to the outside world.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437541162-991672957.png
blocks.alt: NAT: The Bridge Between the Two

blocks.content: 7. A Real World Analogy

Your router public IP address is like a building street address, what mail actually needs to find the right building. Your device private IP address is like an apartment number inside that building, only meaningful once mail has actually arrived at the right building in the first place. The postal service outside never needs to know or care about apartment numbers, only the router acting like the building mail room does.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437541162-346959551.png
8. Why This Split Matters at Internet Scale
blocks.text: 8. Why This Split Matters at Internet Scale

blocks.content: This directly connects back to the IPv4 address scarcity problem covered in the sibling ipv4-vs-ipv6 topic. Private addressing, combined with NAT, lets an entire home or office full of devices share just one single precious public IPv4 address, dramatically stretching the limited supply of public addresses across the billions of devices actually connected to the internet today.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437541162-301407207.png
blocks.alt: Why This Split Matters at Internet Scale
